summary: Jacqueline Maley profiles Melissa Lucashenko, Miles Franklin winner, as she publishes the historical novel Edenglassie, set in 1850s colonial Brisbane and 2024. The article covers the book's inspirations, including Tom Petrie's Reminiscences and the botched hanging of Dundalli, and her view that Aboriginal identity is more than skin colour or ancestry. It also traces her working-class Logan upbringing, discovering at 15 that she is Aboriginal, her early career, and her 2007 divorce and return to poverty.
one_line: Profile of Melissa Lucashenko and her novel Edenglassie, covering colonial Brisbane, Aboriginal identity, and her life from Logan childhood to the Miles Franklin.
key_facts: Melissa Lucashenko is the only person to have won both the Miles Franklin Literary Award and TV's Millionaire Hot Seat.

Her new novel Edenglassie was published by University of Queensland Press; it is a historical epic about Brisbane's shift from penal colony to settler town, when Aboriginal people still outnumbered white colonists.
Lucashenko was inspired in the 1990s by Tom Petrie's Reminiscences of Early Queensland (1904), written by his daughter Constance Petrie.
Edenglassie has two threads: 1850s Mulanyin and Nita, and Brisbane in 2024 with centenarian Eddie, granddaughter Winona and doctor Johnny, who has just discovered his Aboriginal ancestry.

Dundalli evaded capture for 14 years, was convicted in 1854 of two murders and hanged in 1855 on Queen Street; the executioner misjudged the rope and had to swing on the body. He was the last person publicly executed in Queensland.
Census data shows the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander population rose from 548,368 in 2011 to 649,171 in 2016 and 812,728 in 2021, a 25 per cent rise.
Lucashenko won the Miles Franklin in 2019 for Too Much Lip, which judges called 'a novel of celebratory defiance'; her first reaction was 'Bugger me dead!'.
She was born to an Aboriginal mother, Cecile, and a Russian-speaking Ukrainian father, Vladimir Lucashenko (Wally Lucas), and grew up with six older brothers on the outskirts of Logan.
At 15 someone told her she was Aboriginal and to ask her parents; her mother explained that a photo on the dresser was her grandmother.

Her great-grandmother Christina Copson worked as a domestic servant from age eight and was jailed for a week after shooting a man who tried to rape her; she was found not guilty and the Aboriginal man was jailed for six months.
Lucashenko graduated from Griffith University in 1990 with an honours degree in public policy, the first in her immediate family at university.
Her first book, Steam Pigs (1997), won the Dobbie Literary Award; she holds a black belt in karate.

She married Bill, an AusAID foreign aid specialist, and they settled on Bundjalung land in northern NSW until their 2007 divorce, after which she and her daughter moved back to Logan City, poor again.
